description: A timeline comparison of how rapidly liquidity evaporated—and how quickly government backstops and depositor confidence pulled banks back from the brink during the U.S. banking stress cycle.
youtube_description:
🚨 In this chart-race, we replay the U.S. banking stress cycle as deposits, liquidity, and confidence swung—fast. The dramatic part isn’t just who fell. It’s how quickly “safe” institutions absorbed the shock after bailouts and emergency backstops.

🕒 Chapters
00:00 — The calm before the rate shock (2019–2020)
02:05 — Liquidity looks fine… until it isn’t (2021)
03:40 — The rate shock hits balance sheets (2022)
05:30 — Failure ignition: SVB and the contagion template (2023)
07:10 — Second ignition: First Republic collapses (2023)
08:55 — The scramble to absorb risk (late 2023–2024)
10:20 — Recovery diverges: JPM + BofA keep compounding
12:05 — Citi keeps shrinking as the post-stress era hardens (2024–2026)
13:20 — Where the “next” stress would land (2026E)

📈 How to read this visualization
This race tracks a single synthetic “bank stress scoreboard” series (liquidity + depositor confidence proxy) expressed in billions USD. The purpose is narrative clarity: when deposit flight happens, the series collapses; when backstops restore confidence, the series snaps back.

✅ Join the channel for more high-contrast timeline charts.
👉 Comment your pick: which institution do you think would survive the next 200-basis-point shock best?

instagram_caption:
🚀 The “Bank Run” Timeline That Changed Everything—SVB & First Republic in one chart.

Here’s the shock: in the span of months, depositor confidence didn’t just wobble—it evaporated. And once liquidity is gone, history doesn’t wait.

Starting in 2019–2021, the safest institutions (JPMorgan and Bank of America) were steadily compounding their stress resilience—JPM rises from $2,730B in 2019 to $3,350B by 2021, while BofA climbs from $1,650B to $1,850B. Citigroup looks increasingly fragile in comparison, sliding from $780B to $680B as the post-crisis “rebuild” story drifts.

Then the rate shock era hits. By 2022, the scoreboard for JPM jumps to $3,720B and BofA to $2,050B—bigger, diversified balance sheets look sturdier. Citi keeps bleeding, dropping to $620B. Meanwhile, the story for smaller, concentration-heavy banks is quietly building in the background.

In 2023, the timeline turns into a high-contrast disaster movie. Silicon Valley Bank collapses from $110B (2022) to $0B in 2023. First Republic follows the same fate—rising to $140B by 2022, then hitting $0B in 2023. And right after the emergency backstops and depositor action, the “safe absorber” winners accelerate: JPM reaches $4,200B in 2023 and keeps climbing to $4,800B by 2025. BofA follows up the chain: $2,320B (2023) → $2,700B (2025). Citi continues to contract: $540B (2023) → $420B (2025).

By 2026 (estimate), the gap is brutal: JPM at ~$5,050B vs Citi at ~$390B, while SVB and First Republic are, of course, gone.

🔥 Question for you: If regulators signaled a “next-rate-shock” is coming, which bank do you think would capture the most depositor flight next—JPM, BofA, or someone else?
